How to review this project

Three places hold everything. Each step takes about five minutes.

  1. Read this report (you are here): the problem, the data, every notebook, the results and the decisions.
  2. Open the website: glp1-launchlens.streamlit.app. On the home page click “Start here: project guide”, or the green “Open the app” button for a numbered list of all pages. Every page starts with a “This page answers” box and a “How to read this page” panel.
  3. Check the code and notebooks: GitHub repository. The README has the architecture, setup and results; the notebooks/ folder holds the 16 notebooks with their outputs (links per notebook below).

The first visit to the website can take about a minute if the free server was asleep: click “Yes, get this app back up” and wait. Live AI-writing features are switched off online because they need about 6 GB of memory; their evaluated outputs are shown instead.

The project in brief

LaunchLens is an open-source AI analytics platform for pharma sales-optimization teams, built on real public US data, for the 2026 GLP-1 market shift: which doctors to prioritise, why, and what to discuss.

The problem

In 2026 the US GLP-1 market changed twice: Foundayo (orforglipron), the first GLP-1 weight-loss pill, was approved in April, and Medicare began paying for GLP-1 weight-loss treatment through the GLP-1 Bridge in July. Sales teams must re-decide which doctors to see and what to say. The evidence exists but is scattered: 28 million prescription rows, payment records, research papers, FDA labels, side-effect reports and unstructured visit notes.

What was built

One pipeline from raw public data to a live app: a profile for every doctor (HCP 360), a transparent targeting score, NLP models that read visit notes, a cited question-answering system (RAG) and a tool-using AI agent. Every model is measured against a simple baseline, and the failures are published.

What is new, and what is not

The product idea is not new: Veeva, ZS and IQVIA sell similar tools inside companies. The contribution is doing it openly, on real public data, with honest evaluation, focused on 2026, plus an open synthetic visit-notes dataset (real field notes are never public).

Who it is for

Analysts (main users): market and targeting pages. Sales reps (secondary): pre-visit brief and visit log.

3Marketopen ↗

Where is the opportunity? Brand sizes, a state map, and the Medicaid trend to Q1 2026.

Answers: Where is the GLP-1 opportunity, and what drives it?

  • Claims by brand: one bar per brand, Medicare 2024. Colour = molecule. Ozempic (9.93M) is about twice Mounjaro (4.69M). Wegovy is tiny because Medicare did not pay for weight loss in 2024; the July 2026 Bridge changes that.
  • State map: tirzepatide share of tirzepatide + semaglutide claims. Violet = above the 30% US average, teal = below. Hover a state for its numbers. Range: Rhode Island 15% to Utah 45%.
  • Medicaid trend (to Q1 2026): prescriptions per quarter in thousands. Dashed lines are the weight-loss brands. The orange band marks January 2026, when four states ended obesity coverage.
  • Zepbound + Wegovy change by state: orange bars are those four states (PA −96%, NH −88%, CA −76%, SC −62%); nationally about −45%.
  • Claims by specialty: each label reads “claims · tirzepatide share · % of these doctors who prescribe GLP-1”.

What it means: Insurance coverage decides volume. The Medicare Bridge flips the same switch on for patients aged 65+.

Source: Notebook 04 · Medicare Part D 2024, Medicaid State Drug Utilization to Q1 2026

4Find doctorsopen ↗

Who to visit first? All 308,303 doctors ranked by a transparent score, with filters.

Answers: Which doctors should a team prioritise for the 2026 opportunity?

  • Score (0–100): potential 30% · GLP-1 experience 20% · headroom 15% · tirzepatide openness 15% · oral affinity 10% · research 5% · coverage gap 5%. Each part is scaled 0–1 before weighting.
  • Filters: state, specialty, segment, and “No industry contact” (no payment from either GLP-1 maker in 2024–25).
  • Four numbers: doctors in view, their diabetes claims, the median score, and the % with no industry contact. They update with the filters.
  • Table: rank, score and three plain-English reasons per doctor. “Download this list” exports it as CSV.
  • Segments: A champions · B high-value swing (highest average score, 74) · C competitor strongholds · D untapped · E developing · F low volume.

What it means: A team can narrow 308,303 doctors to a short, explainable list. The score decides who receives label-consistent information first, never what a doctor should prescribe.

Source: Notebook 05 · HCP 360 (notebook 03)

5Doctor 360open ↗

Why this doctor? Type a last name (try “Jeet”) to see one profile and its score breakdown.

Answers: Why is this doctor ranked where they are?

  • Type a last name (try “Jeet” or “Anwar”) or a 10-digit NPI.
  • Header: specialty, place, segment, score and rank out of 308,303.
  • Four numbers: diabetes claims 2024, GLP-1 claims, GLP-1 as a % of diabetes prescriptions, industry payments from both GLP-1 makers.
  • Why this score: points each of the 7 components contributes; the bars add up to the score.
  • Evidence: plain-English reasons, plus linked papers or trials (matched by name, so verify).

What it means: Nothing is hidden: every point of the score can be traced.

Source: Notebooks 03 and 05

6Pre-visit briefopen ↗

What should the rep say? The doctor's numbers, verbatim FDA-label facts, likely objections.

Answers: What should a sales rep know before visiting this doctor?

  • Pick a state, optionally a specialty and the product, then one of the top 20 doctors. Default: Ohio, rank 35.
  • Four numbers: rank and score, diabetes claims, GLP-1 claims (and their % of diabetes prescriptions), tirzepatide share.
  • What the label says: sentences quoted verbatim from the FDA label with section and date. The boxed warning is always shown.
  • What similar doctors raise: the share of synthetic visit notes (same specialty) mentioning each objection.
  • Draft with AI: the RAG pipeline; switched off online because the LLM needs ~6 GB of memory.

What it means: Numbers come from code and label facts from the label itself, so the brief cannot invent claims.

Source: Notebooks 05, 09, 13, 14

7Log a visitopen ↗

What happens after? Four NLP models read a visit note and flag possible side effects.

Answers: Can AI read a visit note and catch what matters?

  • Edit the sample note or type your own; results update instantly.
  • Adverse-event check: probability that the note describes a side effect; above the threshold it says “route to safety review”. Tuned for ≥90% recall.
  • Highlighted note: violet = drug, coral = side effect, amber = dose (BiomedBERT NER). Hover a tag for its confidence.
  • Side-effect context: none / concern / reported / negated, with confidence (BERT).
  • Objections raised: e.g. cost, needles, efficacy (TF-IDF + logistic regression).

What it means: Reps' notes are rarely read at scale; this flags safety-relevant notes and doctor concerns automatically.

Source: Notebooks 07, 11, 12 · trained on ADE Corpus v2 and synthetic notes

8Safetyopen ↗

What side effects are reported to the FDA? Context for doctors' questions, not drug comparison.

Answers: What side effects are reported to the FDA for each GLP-1?

  • Pick molecules with the buttons. Top chart: reports received per quarter. Bars: the 10 most-reported reactions per molecule.
  • Tirzepatide's top report is “incorrect dose administered” (29,672): pen and dosing questions, not a new medical signal.
  • Foundayo (orforglipron) has 728 reports, almost all in 2026, because it is new.

What it means: FAERS counts show reporting, not how often side effects happen (voluntary, unverified, no denominator). Use it to anticipate doctors' questions, never to compare drug safety.

Source: openFDA FAERS, collected in notebook 01

9Ask AIopen ↗

Can I just ask? 21 graded example questions answered by the AI agent, with every step shown.

Answers: Can a manager ask questions in plain English?

  • Example questions (instant): 21 questions run once and graded by hand: 12 correct, 5 partial, 4 wrong. Pick one to see the answer, its grade, and each tool the agent called with the data it got back.
  • Ask your own (live): runs the real agent; switched off online (needs ~6 GB of memory; 1–3 minutes per question on a laptop).

What it means: The LLM chooses the tool; code computes every number, and doctor names are never shown.

Source: Notebook 15 · evaluated in notebook 17

10Key numbersopen ↗

The one-screen summary: four numbers and three findings.

Answers: What are the headline numbers and findings?

  • 199,831 GLP-1 prescribers · 19.6M GLP-1 claims (US$24.6bn gross spend) · 30.1% tirzepatide share · 23% of the 10,000 most Bridge-ready doctors had no payment from either GLP-1 maker.
  • Three findings: coverage decides volume; share swings 2.5× by state; high-value doctors are under-reached.

What it means: Prescribing is Medicare 2024; trends to Q1 2026 are Medicaid; the 2026 opportunity is modelled, not observed.

Source: Notebooks 02–05

Notebooks: what each one did

A learning ladder: data → NLP basics → transformers → retrieval → RAG → agents → evaluation. Each notebook explains the theory in plain language, applies it, and saves what the next one needs.

01Data collection from public APIsData

Why: Gather every public source the project needs, reproducibly.

What was done: Reusable, resumable downloaders for openFDA labels and FAERS, PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, Medicaid, Open Payments, the NPPES registry and the ADE Corpus. The 4.4 GB Medicare file is downloaded manually.

Key result: 9 public sources in data/01_raw (never edited). E.g. 8,900 PubMed papers, 1,871 trials, 9 FDA labels.

Decision: Raw data stays untouched; every change happens in code (raw → interim → processed).

Used on the website: Feeds every page

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

02Medicare Part D: GLP-1 filter and profileData

Why: The Medicare file has 28 million rows, too big for pandas or Excel.

What was done: DuckDB SQL streams the 4.43 GB CSV from disk and keeps 7 GLP-1 generic names.

Key result: 420,364 GLP-1 rows and 199,831 prescribers in about 1 minute; 19,620,006 GLP-1 claims.

Decision: DuckDB instead of pandas: query big files without loading them into memory.

Used on the website: Home, Market

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

03HCP 360: one row per doctorData

Why: Prescribing, specialty, payments and research sit in different files.

What was done: Joins five sources on the NPI; drops deactivated NPIs; code assertions check that totals reconcile.

Key result: hcp_360.parquet: 316,559 doctors × 61 columns; 99.6% of NPIs matched the registry.

Decision: One table as the single source of truth for the app, the score and the agent.

Used on the website: Find doctors, Doctor 360

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

04GLP-1 market landscapeData

Why: Understand the market before modelling it.

What was done: Seven charts: brands, states, specialties, the Medicaid trend, coverage cuts, FAERS and research momentum.

Key result: Ozempic 9.9M vs Mounjaro 4.7M claims; tirzepatide share 18% (Oregon) to 45% (Utah); Medicaid obesity GLP-1s grew 27× then fell 40–50% in one quarter when four states ended coverage (Jan 2026).

Decision: “Coverage decides volume” became the core story: the July 2026 Medicare Bridge is the same lever, reversed.

Used on the website: Market, Key numbers

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

05Doctor segmentation and targetingData

Why: Rank doctors for the 2026 opportunity, in a way a manager can explain.

What was done: A 0–100 weighted score from 7 components, 3 plain-English reasons per doctor, 6 segments, a ±20% weight-jitter robustness test, and k-means as a cross-check.

Key result: 308,303 doctors scored. 96.5% of the top 10,000 stay in the top 10,000 under random weight changes (Spearman 0.999). k-means (silhouette 0.50) found a 35k-doctor oral-semaglutide group.

Decision: A transparent weighted score, not a black-box model: there is no ground-truth label for “good target”, and reps must see why.

Used on the website: Find doctors, Doctor 360

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

06NLP foundations: text preprocessingNLP basics

Why: Turn research abstracts and labels into clean text for classical NLP.

What was done: Tokenisation, lemmatisation (spaCy), regex for doses and numbers, stop words (keeping negations), Zipf's law.

Key result: A reusable clean() function and the cleaned research/label corpus (6,160 abstracts after de-duplication).

Decision: Keep negations (“no nausea” ≠ “nausea”), and keep raw text for transformers, which need it.

Used on the website: Groundwork for notebooks 07–08

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

07Classical NLP: TF-IDF baselinesNLP basics

Why: Set an honest baseline that every later model must beat.

What was done: TF-IDF + logistic regression for adverse-event sentence detection; stratified splits, cross-validation, a recall-first threshold, and a leakage check.

Key result: Baseline F1 0.687. Duplicates had inflated cross-validated F1 to 0.84; after de-duplication it was 0.72.

Decision: Always remove near-duplicates before splitting, and evaluate on the test set only once.

Used on the website: Home → Proof (0.69 baseline)

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

08Word embeddings and topic modellingNLP basics

Why: Find research themes and link doctors to them.

What was done: Word2Vec and fastText trained on PubMed; LDA vs BERTopic; emerging-topic trends.

Key result: Domain word vectors, research topics, and research-theme profiles for 736 doctors.

Decision: Word vectors have one meaning per word, so later steps use contextual transformers.

Used on the website: Research signal in the score

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

09Synthetic visit notesData for NLP

Why: Real sales-rep visit notes are confidential, but the rep tools need them.

What was done: 1,200 scenarios fixed the labels first; Qwen2.5-7B (open, free Colab GPU) wrote the notes; a rule-based quality gate rejected bad notes; NER tags came from lexicon matching.

Key result: An open dataset of 1,055 labelled notes (738 train / 159 validation / 158 test) with a dataset card.

Decision: Labels before text, so labels are correct by construction. Weakness stated openly: models trained on synthetic notes will look better than on real notes.

Used on the website: Log a visit, Pre-visit brief

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

10Transformers explainedTransformers

Why: Understand the models before fine-tuning them.

What was done: Self-attention written in NumPy and checked against PyTorch; positional encoding; encoder vs decoder; fill-mask and attention heads in real BERT.

Key result: Concept demos and a comparison of the models used (BERT/BiomedBERT ~110M parameters, Qwen2.5 1.5B and 7B).

Decision: Encoders (BERT) for classification and tagging; decoders (Qwen) for writing answers.

Used on the website: Theory behind notebooks 11–15

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

11Fine-tuning visit-note classifiersTransformers

Why: Classify each note's objections and side-effect context.

What was done: Fine-tuned BERT and BiomedBERT with the Hugging Face Trainer (lr 3e-5, 4 epochs, batch 16) and compared them with TF-IDF using bootstrap 95% intervals.

Key result: Side-effect context: BERT macro-F1 0.97 (TF-IDF 0.86). Objections: TF-IDF 0.94 beat BiomedBERT 0.91.

Decision: Pick the model per task by test results: transformers where context matters (negation), TF-IDF where keywords suffice. The app uses both.

Used on the website: Log a visit

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

12NER and adverse-event detectionTransformers

Why: Highlight drugs, side effects and doses, and flag possible adverse events for safety review.

What was done: BiomedBERT token classification (BIO tags) on visit notes; BiomedBERT sentence classifier on the ADE Corpus (20,896 sentences), with the threshold set for at least 90% recall.

Key result: NER entity F1 0.98 (drug 1.00, side effect 0.95). Adverse-event F1 0.90 vs 0.69 baseline; at 92% recall 73 false alarms instead of 673.

Decision: Tune for recall: missing a real adverse event is worse than a false alarm.

Used on the website: Log a visit, Home → Proof

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

13Sentence embeddings and vector searchRetrieval

Why: The AI must find the right label passage or paper before answering.

What was done: Chunked labels, papers and notes (200 words, 40 overlap) into 8,013 chunks; compared BM25, MiniLM, BGE and a hybrid with rank fusion, a cross-encoder re-ranker and a brand filter; FAISS index.

Key result: Hybrid recall@5: 0.97 on label questions (BM25 0.73) and 0.87 on papers.

Decision: Hybrid search: keywords catch exact drug names, embeddings catch meaning, and each fails differently.

Used on the website: Pre-visit brief, Ask AI

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

14RAG: cited answers and the pre-visit briefGeneration

Why: Answer label questions without inventing facts.

What was done: Qwen2.5-1.5B on CPU answers only from retrieved passages, with citations; an NLI model checks each sentence; a guard blocks or flags unsupported answers.

Key result: 21/30 correct with retrieval vs 4/30 for the same model alone; 77% of sentences supported (29% without).

Decision: Code writes the facts and always adds the boxed warning; the LLM only does small cited steps.

Used on the website: Pre-visit brief, Home → Proof

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

15LLM agent: Ask AIAgents

Why: Let a user ask questions in plain English across all the data.

What was done: An agent with 5 tools (doctor ranking, market summary, side-effect reports, label answers, note search); code computes every number; up to 3 tool calls.

Key result: 12/21 answers fully correct; right tool 81%, right tool and filters 71%; 127 of 128 numbers traceable to a tool.

Decision: After a real failure (a hazard ratio of 0.80 read as “80% reduction”), code-enforced provenance (finalize) now carries tool warnings to the user.

Used on the website: Ask AI

read the notebook with outputs · GitHub

16LoRA fine-tuning (planned)Fine-tuning

Why: Adapt a small LLM cheaply to the domain.

What was done: Planned for a free Colab GPU; not run yet.

Key result: Not done.

Decision: Listed as future work rather than claimed.

Used on the website: —

17Evaluation, guardrails and fairnessEvaluation

Why: One honest scorecard for the whole project.

What was done: 95% intervals for every result, an LLM-as-judge check against human grades, 10 guardrail tests including prompt injection, and a fairness audit of the targeting list.

Key result: LLM judge agrees with humans only 52% (κ 0.28). Guardrails 7/10; 1 of 3 prompt injections worked. Nurse practitioners are under-represented in the top list (0.69×).

Decision: Publish the failures with the successes; humans grade, not a small LLM.

Used on the website: Home → Proof

Design decisions and why

#DecisionInstead ofWhyNotebook
1Use real public US dataSynthetic market data; Kaggle datasetsResults reflect the real 2024 Medicare market. Limitation: Medicare covers people 65+, and 2024 is the latest doctor-level year.01–04
2DuckDB for the 28M-row filepandas, SparkRuns SQL on a 4.4 GB file from disk on a laptop in about a minute; pandas would run out of memory, Spark is overkill.02
3One table per doctor joined on NPI (HCP 360)Separate tables per pageOne source of truth: the score, the app and the agent all read the same numbers.03
4Transparent weighted score, not a machine-learning rankerSupervised model; pure clusteringNo ground-truth “good target” label exists, and managers must explain a ranking. Robustness was tested (96.5% stable); k-means was used only as a cross-check.05
5Company-neutral “industry contact” signalPayments from one company onlyCounts payments from either GLP-1 manufacturer; the project takes no company's side.03, 05
6Synthetic visit notes with labels fixed firstScraping notes; hand-writing notesReal notes are confidential. Fixing labels before generating text makes them correct by construction; a quality gate removes bad notes.09
7Baselines first, then transformersGoing straight to BERTA model only matters if it beats a simple baseline. TF-IDF stayed in use where it won (objections).07, 11
8Remove duplicates before splittingRandom splitDuplicates inflated F1 from 0.72 to 0.84 (leakage); the honest number is reported.07
9Adverse-event threshold for ≥90% recallDefault 0.5 thresholdMissing a side effect is worse than a false alarm; BiomedBERT keeps false alarms low (73 vs 673).12
10Hybrid BM25 + BGE retrieval with a brand filterKeyword-only or embedding-only searchEach method fails on different questions; together recall@5 reaches 0.97; the filter guarantees the right drug's label.13
11Small open LLM on CPU (Qwen2.5-1.5B)Paid API (GPT, Claude)Free, private and reproducible; no data leaves the machine. Cost: weaker reasoning, measured openly.14, 15
12Code writes facts; the LLM only phrasesLet the LLM write the whole briefNumbers come from code; the boxed warning is added by metadata so it can never be dropped; an NLI guard checks sentences.14
13Agent numbers must come from tools (finalize)Trust the LLM's textA real failure (HR 0.80 read as “80% reduction”) showed the LLM can distort tool output; code now attaches provenance.15
14Humans grade the LLM testsLLM-as-judge onlyThe small judge agreed with humans only 52% (κ 0.28) and was too lenient.17
15Free hosting: Streamlit Cloud + Hugging FacePaid server; Hugging Face Docker Space (needs PRO)Free and public. The live LLM features need ~6 GB of memory, so they are switched off online; the 21 evaluated agent runs are shown instead.App

Limitations and future work

  • Visit notes are synthetic, so note models will score lower on real notes.
  • Hand-graded LLM tests are small (21–30 questions), so their intervals are wide (about ±0.15).
  • The 1.5B LLM follows instructions loosely and can invent answers to leading questions.
  • Prompt injection worked once in 3 tries: a planted document could make the system claim off-label use.
  • Medicare covers people 65+ and the latest doctor-level data is 2024; the 2026 opportunity is modelled.
  • The score ranks individuals and under-weights team-based prescribers such as nurse practitioners.
  • Guardrails are demonstrations, not a validated compliance or safety system.

Next steps: LoRA fine-tuning (notebook 16) on a free GPU; a larger LLM for RAG and the agent; a human check of 100 synthetic notes; screening documents against prompt injection; testing on real, consented field notes.

Glossary

GLP-1
A drug class that copies a gut hormone, lowering blood sugar and appetite. Treats type 2 diabetes and obesity.
Semaglutide / tirzepatide
The two leading molecules. Semaglutide (Novo Nordisk): Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy. Tirzepatide (Eli Lilly): Mounjaro, Zepbound.
Foundayo (orforglipron)
A GLP-1 weight-loss pill approved in April 2026.
Medicare Part D
US government drug insurance for people aged 65+. CMS publishes prescriptions per doctor per drug yearly; 2024 is the latest.
Medicaid
US government insurance for low-income people. State-level data runs to Q1 2026.
GLP-1 Bridge
Medicare's 2026 programme paying for GLP-1 weight-loss treatment, from July 2026.
Claim
One filled prescription (including refills) in Medicare data.
HCP / NPI
Health-care professional (any prescriber) / the 10-digit ID every US prescriber has. All tables join on NPI.
HCP 360
Our one-row-per-doctor table: 316,559 doctors × 61 columns from five public sources.
Tirzepatide share
Tirzepatide claims ÷ (tirzepatide + semaglutide claims). US average 30.1% in 2024.
Open Payments
Public CMS records of industry payments to doctors. We use it as a company-neutral “industry contact” signal.
FAERS
The FDA's voluntary adverse-event (side-effect) reporting system. Counts show reporting, not rates.
Adverse event (ADE)
A harmful effect after taking a drug. Companies must collect and report them.
F1 score
0 to 1. Balances catching real cases (recall) and avoiding false alarms (precision). Higher is better.
Recall@5
How often the right document appears in the top 5 search results.
TF-IDF
A classic text method that counts informative words. Our baseline for every text task.
BERT / BiomedBERT
Transformer language models. BiomedBERT was pre-trained on medical papers. We fine-tuned both.
NER
Named-entity recognition: tagging words as drug, side effect or dose.
RAG
Retrieval-augmented generation: the AI first searches documents, then answers only from them, with citations.
Agent
An AI that chooses which tool (program) to run, with which inputs, to answer a question.
95% interval
